Exploring NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning: Making it see with little resources

Open-weight models such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning allow cost-efficient, self-hosted inference for small and large businesses while also allowing for substantial customization. As a self-hosting software company with a track record of customizing LLMs, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning sparked our interest.
For context, TNG is a software consultancy with 930 employees in Munich. We provide LLM inference in Europe with currently more than 250 GPUs in service. Our inference endpoints serve more than 10 billion tokens per day. We host the latest open-weight models available, such as Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and the latest Nemotron variants. Before using it, each new model is thoroughly tested through a comprehensive set of benchmarks that we put together from a list of industry best practice benchmarks. Our models are hosted in a highly secured cluster with zero data retention, a no-log policy and served from within Germany. We use hardware based Confidential Computing if extra security requirements are needed. Our research department has created models of their own based on model merges and post training of existing models, making the models more efficient than their parents in token usage or adding extra capabilities.
We were thrilled to get an early-access version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for testing and tinkering. After running our standard set of checks and benchmarks, we found it to be a highly efficient model and indeed observed the hybrid Mamba architecture paying off. Therefore, this model proved to be a promising candidate for further experiments. Not only can it be run on rather modest resources. Even a smaller GPU such as an RTX 6000 Pro suffices to run fine-tunes and, hence, customize the model for specific use cases at little cost. As a proof of concept for this flexibility, we decided to extend our given checkpoint with vision capabilities, rendering it multi-modal.

How to get Vision Capabilities into a Non-Vision LLM on the cheap

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni provides a full recipe on how to extend a model with multi-modal capabilities, more precisely, how to incorporate the NVIDIA C-Radiov4-H vision encoder to extend NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano with multi-modal capabilities. However, for the scope of our small PoC, we had no intention of training a fully fledged Omni version of NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, which would have required several training phases on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Instead, we decided to go for a simplified approach that is more feasible on limited resources. Most recently, GLM-5.2 Vision demonstrated how a Vision Tower like Kimi K2.6 can be injected into an LLM like GLM-5.2 with minimal training. We decided to adapt this approach to NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.
In separate experiments, we injected both the Kimi K2.6 Vision Tower and NVIDIA C-Radiov4-H. Following the recipe from GLM-5.2 Vision, the essential idea is not to train an entire vision encoder, but fully re-use an existing one and only train the absolute bare minimum: a small MLP adapter. Why is this enough? These vision encoders are perfectly capable, they simply might not fit the way our target LLM works - or, more technically, they might work in a totally different embedding space. This suggests that only the final projection in an existing vision encoder requires adaptation, namely the one that translates the encoder's representation into the target LLM's embedding space. This projection layer is just a small fraction of the vision encoder, and even smaller compared to the full LLM.

   
   Figure 1: Outline of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning extended with Vision Encoder

As a unimodal model, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can only process text input. The input text is first decoded into tokens, each of which is then associated with a certain direction in the model's embedding space. In simple terms, the vision module now has several tasks (cf. Figure 1):

Parse an image provided (optionally) by the user.

De-compose it into a sequence of spatial patches (in analogy of text tokens).

Embed and process those spatial patches in the vision module's embedding space.

The final representations then needs to be projected into the actual LLM's embedding space, where they can be concatenated with the text input's representations.

For our experiments, only part 4) of the image pipeline, the projector, needs to be trained, since everything else is already provided by the used existing vision modules. This way, only 34 million (Kimi K2.6) - 40 million (NVIDIA C-Radiov4-H) parameters instead of hundreds of millions of parameters needed to be trained. Our train runs used around 100 million tokens.

Experiments

We ran all our trainings on entry-level server GPUs (RTX 6000 Pro). While fine-tuning would be feasible on a single GPU, we used 8 for faster training times through data parallelism. We experimented with the Nemotron Image Training v3 dataset as well as the Cauldron dataset.
To track training progress, we prompted our model with the image of Figure 2 together with the prompt "What could this image mean?" every 500 steps.

   
   Figure 2: Example Image Prompt - "What could this image mean?"

   Figure 3: MMMU Benchmark (all models without reasoning)

To verify general vision capabilities, we ran a quick MMMU Benchmark. While falling short of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni scores, we find those results very convincing given how little time for training and data preparation was invested on our side.
For comparison, we also ran a comparative fine-tune on Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B . NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning had a 50% higher token throughput compared to Qwen during fine-tuning.
As an example use case for adding vision capabilities, we fine-tuned Nemotron 3.5 Lightning on medical imaging. We tested the model on imageclef-medical-vqa-2019 as an example of a dataset for medical imaging. For this task, we decided to do a full fine-tune of the vision encoder (i.e. all parts 1 - 4 in Figure 1) to enhance its capabilities in the medical domain. Even with a comparatively small number of trained
images, we observed a significant improvement of the answers on our validation dataset from 20% to 58%. While, of course, these are not conclusive results, we find this to be a strong indication for the general practicality of this approach.

Conclusion

We find NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to be a great open-weight model that - besides many other properties - is particularly well suited for customization via fine-tuning due to its high training efficiency. With just a few days of tinkering and a couple of GPU hours we were able to extend it with fundamental vision capabilities and we are convinced that a lot more can be done from there. Thus, we look forward to further customization, with many ideas in our pipeline.
We thank NVIDIA for providing us with this wonderful opportunity and the very kind support throughout our experiments.
